summary: Gives guidelines to domain registries and registrars on registering internationalized domain names for European languages written in Cyrillic, including Russian, Ukrainian, Bulgarian, Serbian and others. It describes which characters are suitable and discusses variants, including look-alike characters from other scripts. It is an informational, independent submission.

eli5.summary: Web addresses can use letters from many alphabets. This is a rulebook for the people who hand out names written in Cyrillic, saying which letters are fine and how to avoid confusing look-alikes.

subtitle: Character and variant guidelines for domain names written in Cyrillic

tldr.problem: Domain names can now use Cyrillic characters, allowing registrations in Russian, Ukrainian, Bulgarian and other European Cyrillic-using languages. However, Cyrillic letters look very similar to Greek and Latin letters, creating opportunities for confusion and impersonation.
tldr.mechanism: This document provides a table of which Cyrillic characters should be allowed in domain registrations and which Greek or Latin characters they resemble. It defines how registries should handle variants—automatically registering look-alike versions of a name to prevent cybersquatting.
tldr.outcome: Registries can use these guidelines to make consistent policy decisions about Cyrillic IDNs, reducing confusion while allowing legitimate registrations across multiple languages.

today: RFC 5992 is an Informational specification providing guidelines for domain registry administrators. These recommendations remain the reference for handling Cyrillic IDN registrations in the DNS and for managing variant characters that might cause user confusion.

sections.title: The Challenge of Cyrillic Domain Names
sections.content:
The Domain Name System can now support names written in many alphabets, including Cyrillic, the script used by Russian, Bulgarian, Ukrainian, Serbian and other European languages. But Cyrillic shares a big problem with Latin and Greek: the letters look nearly identical. A Cyrillic 'A' and a Latin 'A' are almost indistinguishable on a screen.

When different languages mix in the same DNS zone (which happens with generic top-level domains like .com), the risk grows that an attacker could register a look-alike domain to deceive users—registering the Cyrillic version of a famous site and hoping people cannot tell the difference. This document provides guidelines for the registries that control domain names, helping them make consistent decisions about which Cyrillic characters to allow, and what to do about look-alikes.
sections.eli5: Cyrillic and Latin letters look really similar. If someone registers a fake domain that looks just like a real one in a different alphabet, people might visit the wrong site by mistake.

sections.title: Similar Characters and Variant Registration
sections.content:
Some characters in different scripts have identical or nearly identical visual appearance. When someone registers a domain name containing a character, a registry might want to prevent confusion by automatically registering all the look-alike versions too—the same name written with visually similar characters from other scripts. This practice is called variant registration.

The RFC draws from the variant approaches used for Chinese domain names (which has a long history of managing similar-looking characters) and describes how this strategy applies to Cyrillic. The registry makes a policy choice: it might automatically register all variants to the same person, or it might register one and block the others. The document identifies the specific character pairs that need this special handling.
sections.eli5: When you register a word, the registry can automatically reserve the look-alike versions in different alphabets so nobody else can trick people with a fake version.

sections.title: Character Sets for Different Languages
sections.content:
Cyrillic is not a single alphabet; it is a script with different subsets of characters for different languages. The document defines a Base Cyrillic set of 23 characters that all nine covered languages share, plus additional characters for each language. Russian adds 10 more characters to reach 33 total. Ukrainian may use 31 to 34, Bulgarian 30, and Serbian and Bosnian 30 each. Kildin Sami, an indigenous language of northern Russia and Scandinavia, has a much more complex orthography with 56 characters, some requiring combining marks (accents written separately in the encoding).

Each language section in the document lists its characters by Unicode code points and names. The RFC notes that while Cyrillic is the primary script for these languages, Latin script is often used instead or alongside Cyrillic on keyboards in the same countries. However, the document strongly recommends against mixing Cyrillic and Latin characters in the same domain name label, because the confusion is nearly certain.
sections.eli5: Different European languages that use Cyrillic don't use exactly the same letters. Russian has 33, Ukrainian 31 to 34, Bulgarian 30, and Kildin Sami has 56 with extra marks.

sections.title: Variant Registration and Processing
sections.content:
When a registry receives a domain registration request, it begins with an input label (the name as typed). The registry processes this label through a variant table that lists all allowed characters and the variants that might be visually similar. The processing produces either a failure (the label cannot be registered) or a registration bundle—a set of related domain names, all in standard (A-label) form, that should be registered together to prevent confusion.

The variant table in Appendix A has four columns: the Cyrillic character and its Unicode code point, its Unicode name, and then one or two look-alike characters from Latin or Greek script (if they exist). The table notes variants needed only because of case folding (uppercase and lowercase variants of a confusable pair). Each Cyrillic character appears exactly once in the table, ensuring consistent handling. The registry uses these tables to make its policy decision—which strategy to employ for managing variants—and documents it clearly so users understand what happens when they register.
sections.eli5: The registry looks up each letter and checks if it has a look-alike in another alphabet. If it does, the registration system can automatically protect the look-alike spellings too.
